article.title: Severe El Niño Flooding Batters Navajo Nation Communities
article.summary: Native communities across the US south-west are working to recover after intense El Niño rains triggered once-in-a-generation flooding, submerging parts of New Mexico and Utah in toxic sewage waters.

article.content_html:
Historic Rains Submerge Shiprock Neighborhoods

On the night of 23 October, residents in Shiprock, New Mexico, faced unprecedented flooding as the nearby San Juan River surged dangerously close to residential areas. Jimmie Goodman, a 67-year-old Navajo resident, had to evacuate his sister in a green Ford pickup truck as fast-rising waters flooded their driveway and threatened their home. The extreme weather events struck after an unusually dry year marked by New Mexico's hottest summer on record, catching the desert region off guard with sudden flash floods.

Communities across the 27,000-square-mile Navajo Nation reservation—spanning New Mexico, Arizona, and Utah—felt the severe impact of the storms. In Dennehotso, Arizona, emergency personnel executed daring rescues, airlifting and rafting elders as old as 102 to safety as floodwaters disrupted local infrastructure and residential areas.

San Juan River Faces Severe Contamination

  • The San Juan River crested at 21 feet near Shiprock on 23 October, reaching its highest level reported since 1935 and unseen regional levels since 1911.
  • Floodwaters severely damaged several wastewater treatment facilities in New Mexico and Utah, causing untreated sewage to spill directly into the river.
  • San Juan County officials issued strict warnings labeling the waterway a hazardous material situation and advising residents to avoid the river entirely.

Climate Extremes Threaten Vulnerable Desert Regions

The devastating floods highlight the extreme vulnerability of south-west desert infrastructure to sudden, intense weather shifts driven by El Niño patterns. Following months of scorching summer heat and exceptional dryness, the sudden deluge overwhelmed local drainage systems and wastewater plants, transforming natural waterways into biohazards. Local groups and residents continue to band together in recovery efforts, facing long-term environmental and infrastructure challenges in the aftermath of the disaster.
